title: Part-of-Speech Tagging and HMMs
oneLiner: Label every word as noun, verb, adjective and so on, using both the word itself and the labels of its neighbours.

what.html:
Part-of-speech tagging marks each word with its grammatical role. The tricky part: many common words can play several roles ("I can can the can"). A hidden Markov model solves this by combining two kinds of knowledge: which tag tends to follow which, and which words each tag tends to produce.

Everyday versionYou can't see the weather in a diary, only how many ice creams someone ate each day. From the pattern of ice creams, and knowing hot days tend to follow hot days, you guess the hidden weather. Tags are the hidden weather; words are the ice creams.

why.html:
• Tags feed parsing, name finding, lemmatisation, translation and text-to-speech.
  • It is the classic example of labelling a sequence, used again for names, speech and more.
  • It shows why context matters: the same word changes role with its neighbours.

how.title: One label per word
how.html: "the lead paint is unsafe" → determiner, noun, noun, verb, adjective. "lead" is a noun here, a verb in "lead the team".

how.title: Growing and fixed classes
how.html: Nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs welcome new words (selfie, stream). Prepositions, pronouns and articles are a small fixed set. An unknown word is almost always from the growing classes.

how.title: Standard tag lists
how.html: A common English list has 45 tags (NN noun, NNS plural noun, VBD past-tense verb, DT determiner…). A shorter 17-tag list works across many languages.

how.title: Too many combinations
how.html: Just tagging each word with its usual tag gets about 92% right; using context gets about 97%. But with 45 tags, a five-word sentence has 185 million possible tag sequences, far too many to try one by one.

how.title: Chains of states
how.html: A Markov chain says tomorrow depends only on today. Start warm (0.2) and stay warm three times (0.6 each): 0.0432.

how.title: Hidden tags, visible words
how.html: In an HMM the tags form the hidden chain, and each tag produces a word. Multiply the tag-to-tag and tag-to-word probabilities: "the dog barks" as determiner–noun–verb scores 1.44 × 10⁻⁵.

how.title: Learn by counting
how.html: From hand-tagged text, count how often each tag follows another, and how often each tag is a given word, then divide: P(the | determiner) = 3/4 in a three-sentence example.

how.title: Context beats habit
how.html: "race" is usually a noun, but after "to" a verb is about 1,800 times more likely. Together, "to race tomorrow" is about 840 times more likely with race as a verb.

demo.html: Pick how many ice creams were eaten on three days and see all 8 possible hot/cold weather stories ranked by probability. For 3, 1, 3 the winner is hot–cold–hot.

example.html:
Counting from three tagged sentences. Two of the three start with a determiner, so P(DT at start) = 2/3. Determiners appear 4 times and 3 of them are "the": P(the | DT) = 3/4. Two of the 4 determiners are followed by a plural noun: P(NNS | DT) = 1/2.

Supplementary Even at 97% per word, a typical 20-word sentence still has about a 50% chance of containing at least one tagging error.

misunderstandings: Most word types aren't, but many frequent tokens are.
Neighbouring tags matter; find the best sequence.
They're finer but harder; compare on the same tagset.
takeaways: POS tagging = sequence labelling with a tagset (Penn 45, UD 17).
Open vs closed classes; unknown words are open-class.
Ambiguity + Tⁿ sequences → need a sequence model.
HMM: transitions P(t | t′) × emissions P(w | t), learned by counting.
'to race': transition prior beats emission (VB wins ≈ 840×).
thirty: POS tagging labels each token with a tag (the/DT lead/NN paint/NN is/VBZ unsafe/JJ) and supports parsing, NER, lemmatisation and more. Open classes (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) grow; closed classes (prepositions, determiners, pronouns, auxiliaries) are fixed. Penn Treebank has 45 tags; Universal Dependencies 17. Frequent words are ambiguous (I can can the can), so we need the best sequence among Tⁿ (45⁵ ≈ 1.85 × 10⁸). A Markov chain has π and A (warm×4 = 0.2 × 0.6³ = 0.0432). An HMM adds emissions B: P(w, t) = Π P(tᵢ|tᵢ₋₁)P(wᵢ|tᵢ) (the dog barks = 0.06 × 0.00024 = 1.44 × 10⁻⁵), decoding by argmax P(w|t)P(t). Estimate by counts (P(NN|DT) = 600/1000; toy P(the|DT) = 3/4). For 'to race tomorrow', VB (2.7 × 10⁻⁷) beats NN (3.2 × 10⁻¹⁰).
